description: Question: a protein backbone has two free rotations per residue, φ (around N–Cα) and ψ (around Cα–C). Why do proteins fold into a few repeating shapes, helices and sheets, rather than anything at all? Data: the backbone angles of every residue of four well-resolved proteins, myoglobin 1A6M (1.0 Å, all α), T4 lysozyme 2LZM, ubiquitin 1UBQ and green fluorescent protein 1EMA (a β-barrel), as PDBe's validation pipeline (MolProbity) computed them from the coordinates, with PDBe's helix and strand assignments. Steps: residues with φ and ψ per entry, joined to the helix and strand ranges; each residue placed in a region of the plane (α_R, β, PPII, α_L) and in a 10° cell; then the occupancy of the plane, and summaries per secondary structure and for glycine and proline apart. Aha: only a small part of the 360° × 360° square is used, because atoms of neighbouring residues collide everywhere else (Ramachandran, 1963): half of the 606 residues lie in 1.4% of the plane and 95% in 10.6% (10° cells). Helix residues sit in one tight basin (median φ −64°, ψ −40°), strands in another (−120°, +135°); positive φ is glycine's (22 of the 34 residues there; 48% of glycines against 2% of other residues), the one amino acid without a side chain, and proline's ring pins φ at −63° ± 10°. Secondary structure is a run of residues in one basin. Caveats: four proteins (606 residues; alternate conformations, listed twice with the same angles, counted once) are a small sample; the region boxes are approximate (MolProbity's Favored/Allowed contours come from ~100,000 residues and differ per residue type); PDBe's helix/strand ranges come from the deposited annotation; angles are from crystal structures (one conformation). Next: hover a residue; drill down to one protein or residue type; expand to more PDB entries (any id works with the same queries) or to NMR ensembles.
name: The Ramachandran plot: why proteins have helices and sheets
